summary: Defines a ROHC profile for compressing IP/UDP/RTP packets, using help from the link layer so the headers can often be removed entirely during good conditions. It builds on the ROHC RTP profile. It was replaced by RFC 4362.

plainLanguage.summary: If the road already tells everyone who is driving, the car does not need a nameplate. This drops headers where the link already carries the information. It has been replaced by RFC 4362.

questions: how does lla rohc eliminate headers
subtitle: Zero-byte header compression for wireless IP/UDP/RTP using link-layer help.

tldr.problem: ROHC RTP can compress IP/UDP/RTP headers down to one byte, but some wireless links (like GSM and CDMA) are so inflexible about packet sizes that even one byte of header overhead is expensive. The link layer cannot accommodate any extra header.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3242 extends ROHC RTP to send header-free packets in normal operation, replacing the one-byte header with zero bytes. The link layer provides packet type identification, sequence numbering and loss indication to compensate for the missing header.
tldr.outcome: This profile achieves the spectrum efficiency of existing circuit-switched solutions on older wireless systems while remaining fully transparent. It was later replaced by RFC 4362.

today: RFC 3242 defined the Link-Layer Assisted ROHC RTP profile for zero-byte header compression on inflexible wireless systems. It was later replaced by RFC 4362, which refined the profile.

sections.title: The Problem of Inflexible Links
sections.content:
Header compression has long improved efficiency over bottleneck links. ROHC RTP compresses IP/UDP/RTP headers to a single octet, which works well over most networks. However, older wireless systems like GSM and CDMA optimise for specific payload sizes. Adding even one byte forces them to use the next larger fixed packet size, wasting precious spectrum.

Newer air interfaces like WCDMA are flexible enough to use ROHC RTP efficiently. But to support existing vocoders and hardware on older systems, a zero-byte header format is needed. RFC 3242 defines how to achieve this with help from the link layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Older wireless networks were built for voice calls of a fixed size. If you add even a tiny header, the whole packet has to be twice as big. This solution lets the header disappear completely on these networks.

sections.title: The Link-Layer Assisted Approach
sections.content:
The Link-Layer Assisted (LLA) ROHC RTP profile extends the standard ROHC RTP profile (profile 0x0001) by defining profile 0x0005. Instead of a one-byte header, the compressor can send a No-Header Packet (NHP)—just the payload, with zero header bytes.

For this to work, the lower layers must provide three things: packet type identification (to tell an NHP from a normal header), sequence number information (from the link layer's own synchronization), and loss indication (so the decompressor knows when packets were dropped). The link layer MUST guarantee in-order delivery and provide notification of any packet loss.
sections.plainLanguage: The wireless network already knows the sequence of packets and which ones got lost. ROHC can skip the header and rely on the wireless system to carry that information.

sections.title: Packet Types and Context Handling
sections.content:
The LLA profile defines three new packet types beyond standard ROHC RTP packets. A No-Header Packet (NHP) carries only the payload and is used when all header fields are unchanged or follow the established pattern. A Context Synchronization Packet (CSP) carries header information without payload to resync the decompressor if data is discarded. A Context Check Packet (CCP) is sent periodically to verify the decompressor's context by including an optional CRC.

The compressor maintains context and periodically sends verification packets. The decompressor infers the RTP sequence number from the link layer's packet loss indication and uses CRCs from CSP and CCP packets to detect errors, avoiding the reliance on CRCs in every packet that standard ROHC RTP uses.
sections.plainLanguage: The compressor sends three types of packets: mostly bare payloads, occasional headers to sync up, and periodic checks to make sure everything is still working right.

sections.title: Interface Between ROHC and the Link Layer
sections.content:
The compressor delivers to the assisting link layer: the original ROHC RTP packet, a segmentation flag, the new packet type (NHP/CSP/CCP), and the RTP sequence number. The link layer uses this information to decide whether to send the full packet or allow an NHP.

The assisting layer delivers to the decompressor: the received packet, a flag indicating whether it is an NHP, and packet loss indications. This allows the decompressor to maintain proper sequencing even when the header is missing. The RFC emphasizes that additional documents must specify how this interface works for specific link technologies like WCDMA or CDMA2000.
sections.plainLanguage: The compressor tells the wireless system what it is sending and what sequence number it is. The wireless system tells the receiver which packets arrived and in what order.

sections.title: Reliability and Transparency
sections.content:
The LLA profile is fully transparent to any IP/UDP/RTP stream; it does not make assumptions about packet timing or content. It performs optimally for streams synchronized exactly with the link, such as voice at fixed intervals.

Transparency is guaranteed because the assisting layer provides loss indication that was not available in older compression schemes like VJ, IPHC and CRTP. Periodic context verification using CCP packets provides additional protection against undetected bit errors. The profile MUST NOT be used when UDP checksums are enabled (as with IPv6, always enabled for IPv6/UDP).
sections.plainLanguage: As long as the wireless system reliably tells the receiver about lost packets, the compression is safe. Voice calls are the perfect use case, so this profile works especially well for them.
